profile_interpretation: Atlas fields describe designs; capability states are reviewer claims at each report revision. Neither feature presence nor descriptive fields are benchmark performance.

Memory unit.value: A SQLite row for conversation turns and tool logs; an embedded Chroma `Document` with a content-hash id for knowledge, workflow, toolbox, entity and summary; a `MERGE`d Neo4j node when the graph is configured

Storage backend.value: Two SQLite tables — `CONVERSATIONAL_MEMORY` and `TOOL_LOG_MEMORY`, in two separate database files — plus five Chroma collections embedded with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, plus an optional Neo4j entity graph, plus a second, unrelated Chroma collection for the RAG corpus

Retrieval strategy.value: `similarity_search(query, k)` against each Chroma collection and `WHERE thread_id = ?` against the two tables; `AgentMemory.recall` fans out to five of the seven and ranks them by a constant chosen per store, discarding whatever the search ranked

Write strategy.value: Synchronous. A regex on the text picks entity, workflow or knowledge unless `role` or `type` is passed; Chroma writes upsert on a SHA-256 content hash

Update/delete model.value: Delete by id on both tables, a whole thread on the conversational one, `delete_from_store(name, ids)` on any of the five collections, `DETACH DELETE` on graph entities, plus `delete_collection` and `reset_database`. The one `UPDATE` sets `summary_id`, and nothing outside a test calls it

Scoping model.value: `thread_id` filters both SQL read paths and is stamped into entity Chroma metadata, where no read path consults it; no user, project or tenant key anywhere

Agent integration.value: `AgentMemory.remember`/`recall`, plus LangChain `BaseMemory`, `BaseStore[str, str]` and `BaseChatMessageHistory` adapters, plus a standalone agent entry point

Background processing.value: None — no scheduler, no consolidation pass, no expiry

Trust/provenance model.value: None. No status, confidence or provenance field on any store; the one `status` column records whether a tool call succeeded

Notable strengths.value: Seven memory types separated by store rather than by a type column, each annotated with the cognitive category it stands for, behind a two-method API that routes and fans out for the caller

Main risks.value: Recall scores are constants per store, so cross-store ranking is a fixed preference order; enabling Neo4j collapses every entity written through the simple API onto one node named `entity_0`

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: An L4 core fact — key, value, importance, memory kind, visibility, source, metadata, optional expiry — over L3 episodes, an L2 session store, a persisted L1 reflex buffer and an L0 capture journal

Storage backend.value: Plain SQLite in one data directory: core_memory, a core_memory_history ledger, a core_memory_temporal interval table, episodes, an epistemic graph, wiki pages, staged proposals and an archive table

Retrieval strategy.value: Tokenized LIKE search over L4 with visibility and superseded-pair filtering, L3 episode search, and a multi-source retriever over RAG, wiki, episodes, facts, graph and entities; session-start and context tools assemble facts by importance

Write strategy.value: remember(key, value, importance, source, ttl_minutes, visibility, memory_kind) through the MCP tool, plus a distiller and an hourly consolidation sweep that write without a visibility argument; created_at can carry the source message time

Update/delete model.value: A save updates in place by key and appends a ledger row; delete appends a row with a null after-image. Forget moves rows to a shadow archive with dry run and undo; the forgetting loop archives and deletes outside the ledger

Scoping model.value: Layer (user or agent) and user id bound into a handle and applied on every CoreMemory and EpisodicMemory read; the MCP tools take both as arguments. The recall cache key omits the layer

Agent integration.value: An MCP server with a primitive and a flat tool surface, lifecycle hooks and an autohooks daemon, an HTTP surface described by openapi.yaml, and a PyPI package

Background processing.value: A 15-minute loop for decay, archiving and edge pruning under a per-base maintenance lock, hourly compaction and consolidation per layer, and a nightly graph enrichment pass

Trust/provenance model.value: A visibility flag preserved across automatic re-saves, a source provenance contract, a before-and-after ledger on the two CoreMemory mutators, a staged proposal queue the agent decides, and an interval chain no production path reads

Notable strengths.value: The re-save rule is the precise one: an absent visibility argument keeps the stored flag rather than resetting it to the default, so the distiller and consolidation, which never pass one, cannot resurrect a hidden key, and the comment records the bug and date behind it ("F1 sanitation, 2026-09-12"). Search excludes private and hidden in SQL under a named invariant, and committed tests assert both exclusions against a store holding a matching visible or pinned fact. The ledger stores full before and after JSON with an attribution and is never rewritten. Scope is carried by the handle, and the project's own fix for a multi-source retriever that answered the agent layer with user rows added tests asserting both directions

Main risks.value: The visibility predicate lives in three queries and not in get_all, and CoreEntry has no visibility field, so the one Python-side check (features/inject.py:222) always passes. Six context builders render key=value from get_all: two inject blocks, the recall protocol, smart context, memory_context and memory_context_inject, which also writes CONTEXT.md, so a private or hidden fact above the importance threshold reaches a prompt. The agent can clear the flag by passing visibility='visible', and a rollback of a deleted hidden key reinserts it visible. The ledger and the interval chain sit under bare exception handlers and drop silently, the ledger misses every write outside CoreMemory.save and delete, and the interval chain is on the write clock with no production reader. The recall cache key omits the layer, so a recall on one layer serves the other's results for 300 seconds

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: An items row: kind raw (one verbatim message, prefixed with its UTC stamp and speaker) or fact (a gpt-4o-mini first-person sentence, or an update's current-value sentence), with user_id, session_id, request_id, the message timestamp and a vector

Storage backend.value: One SQLite file in WAL mode with items, requests and embedding_metadata, plus updates and update_checks when an update switch is on; a per-user numpy matrix cached in process, evicted least-recently-used past 1,000,000 rows

Retrieval strategy.value: Brute-force cosine over the user's matrix against the question fused 50/50 with a gpt-4o-mini first-person recall question; up to 100 items with each turn's neighbours, verbatim turns ordered first, bounded by top_k, characters and a counted token budget; optional as-of and update withholding

Write strategy.value: Synchronous /add: every message stored verbatim, one gpt-4o-mini extraction of up to 24 facts per chunk, an optional two-stage update detector beside it, all embedded and committed before 200; idempotent per user and request_id

Update/delete model.value: No update or delete path. With the update switches on, an explicitly replaced value is withheld from current-value questions per earlier memory, after a model verdict stored per update and item; a later restatement is returned

Scoping model.value: user_id on every row and a WHERE user_id = ? predicate on every content read, with the cache keyed on it; session_id is stored and never filtered; user_id is supplied by a caller holding one shared bearer secret

Agent integration.value: An HTTP service with /add, /search and /health for the Agent Memory Leaderboard contract, in Docker compose bound to loopback; no agent tools

Background processing.value: None. Update verdicts are computed lazily on the first /search that needs them and persisted; as-of time readings are cached in process

Trust/provenance model.value: No epistemic state. Verbatim turns are the primary source and facts a paraphrase; a replaced value is a per-pair verdict whose effect a question router can cancel, and every failed model call withholds nothing

Notable strengths.value: Two copies of every chunk with provenance-ordered delivery; withholding that only removes stored text, gated by quote containment and failing open; a request deadline, admission valve and token budget that keep each call inside the platform's limits

Main risks.value: Suppression is keyed on earlier memories, so a later restatement of a replaced value returns and only the 20 nearest earlier mentions are judged; nothing can be deleted; the chunk-memory research path ignores withholding; user_id is caller-asserted

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: A fixed-size struct — type, category, importance, certainty, emotional weight, involved entity, location, a forgotten flag — carrying no text at all, beside a belief struct with a status enum and pointers to the memories supporting and contradicting it

Storage backend.value: In-process stores keyed by entity id, serialized whole into JSON world snapshots at a tick interval by a generic resource loop no test exercises for them; no database, despite an ADR selecting SQLite

Retrieval strategy.value: Swappable `IMemoryRetrievalStrategy` implementations, scored by importance decayed against simulation time, over a candidate list the retrieval system flattens out of every entity's memories into one world-level working memory of seven chunks

Write strategy.value: Nothing in the engine writes a memory or a belief. `AddMemory` and `AddBelief` have no caller outside the test suite; the per-tick phases decay, consolidate, retrieve and project a store only a test can fill

Update/delete model.value: `Forgotten` flips when decayed importance falls below a threshold and nothing is destroyed; the belief statuses `Weakening`, `Revised`, `Abandoned` and `Contradicted` are declared in the enum and assigned nowhere in the repository

Scoping model.value: Each store is one list per entity id, so the owner is the container rather than a field on the record — a partition, not a filter. Three reads pass an id; the retrieval system reads every entity's memories at once

Agent integration.value: None shipped. The engine builds a validated `SemanticState` for a language model and the repository contains no client that sends it

Background processing.value: Ordered per-tick systems — perception, attention, working memory, consolidation, long-term decay, reasoning, planning, decision, audit, enforcement — under a deterministic scheduler

Trust/provenance model.value: `BeliefStatus` as a five-value enum beside `BeliefSource` provenance, read as a filter by the extractor and written by nothing — `Active` is the only value assigned anywhere, and only in four test lines

Notable strengths.value: A validator that refuses to hand a model engine internals, asserted on the serialized payload by committed tests; determinism enforced in its own CI job; a test suite half again the size of the engine it covers

Main risks.value: The durable tier has no producer, so every mechanism over it is specified rather than exercised; memory rows carry no content, so nothing can be corrected about what was remembered; the reasoning trace is cleared every tick

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: Three record types per teacher trajectory: a workflow insight of two to four sentences keyed on the task's first message, subtask segments with a label, description and masked example calls, and per-call function records keyed on the tool name

Storage backend.value: A directory per build: workflow documents.json, subtask segments.jsonl and function records.jsonl, each beside a NumPy embedding matrix whose rows must line up with the records

Retrieval strategy.value: Workflow top-1 by cosine over OpenAI text-embedding-3-small of the task's first message; subtask best match per turn instruction above 0.45; function records by exact tool name, ranked by similarity, only after a tool call returns an error

Write strategy.value: Offline batch only: a teacher model runs the benchmark, a builder LLM writes workflow and subtask records per trajectory, function records are copied from the successful calls. The student never writes

Update/delete model.value: None in code. BFCL keeps the first workflow record per task id and appends function records without deduplication; the only delete is rmtree of the whole ToolSandbox memory directory behind a --clear flag

Scoping model.value: One directory per build date, passed as a path. BFCL stores a benchmark category on each record and filters on it, then retries unfiltered when the filter returns nothing

Agent integration.value: Overlay files for three benchmark harnesses: a modified BFCL base_handler.py, a ToolSandbox agent role, and six AppWorld configs naming an agent type that no file in the tree registers

Background processing.value: None

Trust/provenance model.value: None. Every retrieved record is injected as reference material; source is the constant teacher

A ledger whose status transitions append a record carrying `seq`, a nanosecond stamp and a `ref_id` back to the entry, making the transition sequence replayable. Write strategy.value: A salience score sorts each write into active, staging, or kept-but-tagged low-salience; a same-concept match is reinforced instead of duplicated unless the caller names what the write supersedes

Update/delete model.value: Supersession by id or by concept match; retraction flags the row and optionally writes a correction that inherits its strong edges; consolidation and the staging sweep hard-delete expired staged and orphaned archived engrams

Trust/provenance model.value: A confidence float from the extracting model, a reinforcement count, and a two-value tier promoted on reinforcement and age. There is no status, no rejection record and no approval field

Agent integration.value: One Rust binary: CLI, stdio MCP with 29 tools, an HTTP MCP server, a daemon, a Python agent SDK, native bindings for Python, Node, Elixir and C, Claude Code and Hermes plugins, and a separate server binary with REST and a ten-tool HTTP MCP

Update/delete model.value: Every correction writes a successor and retires the old row as superseded; a model edit to user-stated content becomes a pending correction proposal; `facts.retract` and per-turn retraction invalidate by triple, capped by the actor's rank, and write a refusal

Background processing.value: The `memory_facts` extraction drain, re-embedding and index maintenance, the decision revisit sweep, and hygiene previews that queue proposals rather than mutate

Trust/provenance model.value: Authority ranks model 10, system 20, user 30, operator 40, derived from the verified caller and never from text; a model-authored fact is a candidate until an operator approves it or a higher rank re-asserts it; a confidence floor of 0.4 and a PII gate on the fact block

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: An immutable memory version — content, kind, confidence, embedding, writer — addressed by a logical id, with entity and relation edges and an episode beside it

Storage backend.value: One DuckDB file holding memories, edges, episodes, audit rows, a BM25 index and the bundled integration tables, queryable with SQL by anyone who opens it

Retrieval strategy.value: Reference walks over the entity graph, BM25 text ranking and optional vector search, each narrowing a candidate set that is then filtered by the visibility predicate

Write strategy.value: Verbs — remember, relate, supersede, reinforce, forget, unrelate — each inserting a new version rather than editing the row it corrects

Update/delete model.value: A correction closes the current version's transaction interval and inserts the next in the same transaction; `forget(hard=True)` is a right-to-erasure purge that also runs registered hooks over tables anatid does not own

Scoping model.value: `tenant_id` compiled into every read from one module, with a test that fails the build when any other module writes the predicate by hand

Agent integration.value: A Python library, an MCP server, and bundled agent integrations whose tables are covered by the erasure hooks

Background processing.value: Index generations and a journal, with derived accelerators constrained to narrowing rather than answering

Trust/provenance model.value: Provenance through a writer on every version, an audit table with typed counterparts, and erasure that reaches transcripts and serialised state

Notable strengths.value: The enforcement mechanism is the thing to take. Most systems in this corpus hold their scope predicate by convention, and the atlas keeps finding the read path that forgot it. anatid puts the predicate in one module and then writes `test_no_module_writes_the_visibility_predicate_by_hand`, which parses every module's AST, pulls its string literals with docstrings excluded and f-strings handled, and fails when a literal that starts like SQL also matches `tenant_id\s*=\s*(\?|\{)` — one parameterised test per module "so a failure names the file". The same discipline shows in two smaller rules. An accelerator "only ever narrows the candidate set", because "[a]n index built over current state cannot answer what was visible at an earlier instant", so a stale index can cost recall and can never leak a row past the guard. And the audit schema is shaped by erasure: the counterpart memory id "goes in a COLUMN, never into `reason`", because a hard forget "has to be able to find and delete every audit row that names an erased memory, and it cannot search free text for it". `erasure.py` then chases the copies that live outside the memory graph entirely — transcripts, serialised run states — and covers integration tables that are "counters today" so that "a column added later cannot quietly reopen the hole"

Main risks.value: There is no epistemic status: a memory is current or superseded, and the axis that decides is time rather than a judgement, so a claim nobody has verified and one a reviewer confirmed are indistinguishable at read time beyond a confidence number. Nothing is keyed on a rejected value — a hard forget removes every copy it can reach, and re-asserting the same content afterwards produces an ordinary new memory with nothing recording that the store was once asked to erase it. The erasure hooks are the honest version of a hard problem and they are still hooks: coverage of a table anatid has never heard of depends on whoever created it registering one, and the module says so. The usage counters are excluded from the bitemporal rule by design and are mutated in place, so an older version keeps the counts it had when it closed rather than the ones the memory has now. And DuckDB is a single-writer analytical file, which is what makes the SQL-queryable promise real and also what bounds the concurrency this can serve

Intervals are half-open, stated explicitly: "a row closed exactly at T is already invisible at T, and a row opened exactly at T is already visible." Corrections never rewrite: a supersede, soft forget, unrelate or confidence-changing reinforce closes the current version's `tx_to` and inserts the next version in the same transaction, so at most one version of a logical id is selected for any pair of instants. project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: Five element kinds — Concept, Proposition, Assertion, Evidence, Activity — where a Proposition is a claim, an Assertion is somebody claiming it with a stance, a confidence and a world-time window, and Evidence is what the Assertion cites

Storage backend.value: An embedded Rust document database over an object store, with B-Tree, BM25 and HNSW indexes, plus a per-Space version log and a separate governance plane of rows no query can reach

Retrieval strategy.value: KQL patterns over the graph, defaulting to active elements, with BM25 and vector search beneath and a `BELIEF` form that projects rather than reads

Write strategy.value: KML clauses through one transaction path that stamps the engine-owned envelope columns and advances the Space sequence

Update/delete model.value: Lifecycle transitions — archive, quarantine, tombstone, merge, supersede — all additive, plus `PURGE` as the one destructive operation, guarded and digest-stubbed

Scoping model.value: A MemorySpace bound into the session, emitted as a predicate on every read; explicitly not a topic namespace

Agent integration.value: A Rust workspace of fifteen crates, with Python and TypeScript bindings, a server crate and a WASM build of the protocol

Background processing.value: Retention sweeps that tombstone expired elements before purging those already reviewed

Trust/provenance model.value: A projection that computes belief from Assertions under a named policy and never stores it, a governance plane with default deny and bound approvals, and a version log under every change

Notable strengths.value: The governance module's opening line is the sharpest statement of the memory-privilege problem in this corpus: "Cognitive content may describe authority. Only this plane can grant it." A Space can hold a Proposition saying Alice is an administrator, an Assertion supporting it at high confidence and Evidence for both, and Alice administers nothing — because grants are rows no KML clause can reach, "which is what keeps a prompt injection into ordinary memory formation from having a route into policy". The same file separates three questions most systems conflate: should I believe this, am I allowed to touch it, how strongly may it influence what I do. Projection is equally disciplined — belief is "a view, never stored state", because storing it "would create a second answer that could disagree with the Assertions it came from, and nothing would say which one was right" — and its three arithmetic rules are exactly the failures this atlas keeps finding: absence of support is not rejection, saying a thing three times is one voice repeated, and two Assertions citing the same Evidence are not independent because "[m]anufactured corroboration is exactly what an attacker builds". Purge keeps a digest stub because "a dangling reference does not say 'this was erased', it says nothing at all, which is worse for an auditor"

Main risks.value: The cost is that almost nothing here is cheap to adopt. This is 169,548 lines of Rust across fifteen crates implementing a versioned protocol specification, requiring Rust 1.95, with a breaking 1.x to 2.0 migration in this very release — a reader wanting a memory library will find a governed graph database with a query language, a change-envelope model and a policy engine, and no smaller entry point. Approval is separation of duties rather than human review: an approval is signed by a Principal, `allow_self_approval` defaults false so a requester cannot approve their own operation, but nothing requires the approving Principal to be a person, and there is no review console in the tree — so on a host whose Principals are all agents, `RequireApproval` is a second agent's signature. Historical reads are declared scans that "enumerate the version log" because "[t]he indexes on the current rows describe the present", charged against the query budget and refusing rather than stalling on a large Space. And projection is explicit that "Evidence quality is not automatically evaluated" — the arithmetic protects against manufactured corroboration, not against a plausible, well-cited falsehood

Memory unit.value: An `Observation` — one line of text in one layer, carrying `weight`, `decay_rate`, `tags`, `source`, a `memory_state` of new/current/deprecated and a `superseded_by` pointer; beside it an ontology `(entity, key) → value` property and a whole `MemoryFile` with its chunks

Retrieval strategy.value: Two arms that never meet — FTS5 `bm25` or tsvector `ts_rank` across five domains in `MemorySearch`, mapped monotonically to `q/(1+q)` and merge-sorted; and a brute-force in-process cosine scan over the agent's and the global `memory_file_chunks.embedding` in the prompt assembler, with keyword counting as the degraded fallback

Write strategy.value: Observations are written only by a tool call, an admin request or a boot repair; the ontology reconciler writes properties from parsed JSON. The scheduler opens a `consolidation:intake:` session and the LLM must call `consolidation` with `action: "create"`; the intake text reply is discarded, and the created rows are found by diffing the layer's ids before and after

Update/delete model.value: `revise` is copy-on-write with `superseded_by` on the old row and lifts same-text tombstones; `retire` sets `Deprecated` and leaves a row the create path consults by exact text within one layer; `merge` deprecates its sources without superseding them; a boot pass supersedes the newer of two identical live observations. Archive is a hard `DELETE FROM observations` when the model says demote on the bottom layer, with the full row in the mutation log. `ontology:delete` removes an entity with a logged motivation; nothing removes or moves a single property

Scoping model.value: `agent_id` on layers, observations, entities, properties, ontology search docs and diary entries; the layer is the enforced boundary on every observation read path, the ontology's unique key and search arm carry the agent, and a Lua script runs as its VM's bound agent

Agent integration.value: One `animusd` binary — Drogon HTTP API, a Vue 3 admin SPA compiled into the executable, Lua channel adapters, a Lua 5.4 scripting runtime, two agent-facing tools (`memory`, `consolidation`) and an `ActiveMemoryProvider` at priority 30 in the prompt

Background processing.value: Cron schedules per agent and per layer, re-registered on any layer change — hourly intake into `day`, a review pass per layer from every two hours to yearly, and a session-report pass 30 minutes after intake, with `millennium` excluded. At boot, a sweep for live twins of retired rows; a federation pull loop when peers are configured

Trust/provenance model.value: `MemoryState { New, Current, Deprecated }` on an observation and on the ontology property linked to it, filtered out of the assembled prompt, the review batch and unified search; a retired row makes the same text in the same layer arrive deprecated; an ontology property in a selected entity is printed whatever its state

Notable strengths.value: A discrete epistemic state spent on withholding rather than discounting, on four read paths, and a retired row consulted on create so re-extraction lands deprecated. Two append-only mutation logs that both snapshot the row; one predicate for which tools a session is offered and may call; a perspective pass that refuses to run on nothing; write receipts from `INSERT ... RETURNING`; a migration tool that aborts on any column mismatch

Main risks.value: `merge` retires its sources in the tombstone shape, so a merge that keeps a source's wording loses the value at the next boot. The Lua bridge skips the session-type gate and reaches every consolidation verb on its own agent. A revised-away wording is not a tombstone and comes back live on re-derivation. `source` is model-supplied; deprecated ontology properties are searchable and printed; ontology correction is entity-level only; on PostgreSQL a property whose evidence is deleted keeps its state; federation applies a peer's outbox as written

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: A file beneath a namespace mount, indexed for search; atomic facts are additionally extracted from the component's own audit log by a consolidation pass

Storage backend.value: The filesystem, one mount per namespace with its own index of `files` and `files_vec`, plus git auto-commit and tar.gz snapshots for rollback

Retrieval strategy.value: BM25 and dense vectors fused by reciprocal rank fusion with time-decay ranking, over the per-mount index; auto-recall injects relevant context before the next prompt

Write strategy.value: File writes through a kernel-enforced sandbox, optionally auto-committed to git; consolidation is the second writer, extracting atomic facts from the audit log and dropping any candidate whose title or content trips the injection heuristics

Update/delete model.value: No status, no supersession and no tombstone: versioning is git and rollback is a commit or a snapshot, at file or mount level

Scoping model.value: A namespace is a mount with its own root descriptor and its own index, so separation is physical rather than a key composed into a query; every model-supplied path is resolved by the kernel beneath that descriptor via openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH and RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS

Agent integration.value: An MCP server exposing 37 tools, an adapter layer, cgroup limits and a journald audit sink beside the JSONL one; Linux only, requiring a kernel new enough for openat2

Background processing.value: Auto-capture observing at conversation end, a consolidation pass extracting atomic facts from the audit log, an indexing worker, and snapshot and git versioning

Trust/provenance model.value: None as a field. What protects the store is containment and an injection heuristic, not a state a memory can carry: a flagged search hit is annotated and still returned, and a flagged consolidation candidate is dropped without a durable record

Notable strengths.value: The sandbox is enforced by the kernel rather than by a validator, and the module names the symlink-swap attack it exists to stop; coverage is split into two honest tiers with the weaker one labelled best-effort; escape tests assert the file is absent from the target directory rather than that a call errored; and the audit log records failure branches with their errors rather than only successes

Main risks.value: Injection-flagged search hits are annotated and returned rather than withheld, so the decision passes to whatever adapter reads the flag; a rejected consolidation candidate leaves no durable record of the rejection; two of the three namespace kinds are declared and unused, so per-agent separation reads as available when only the user kind is live; and the audit log is per-mount and unsigned

Storage backend.value: The vault's Markdown files are the store of record; a Chroma PersistentClient collection under the XDG data directory holds chunk embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with source, folder, type, tags, links, incoming link count, title and mtime as metadata; a centroid cache and a heartbeat JSON beside it

Retrieval strategy.value: search_vault embeds the query, takes the top n chunks from Chroma (three by default, tripled when a tags filter will trim), optionally prefiltered on frontmatter type, drops chunks below a floor of 0.35 on a (1+cosine)/2 scale, and adds up to 0.20 for a wikilink to or from a context note and up to 0.10 for inbound links; get_connections walks wikilinks breadth-first to depth three

Write strategy.value: Explicit: the agent calls log_note, which writes type/slug.md and returns; a person writes in Obsidian; either is indexed by a separate watcher process that deletes the note's chunks by source path and adds new ones, then rewrites its Related section from a vector query with a relevance margin

Update/delete model.value: An edit to the file replaces all of the note's chunks on the next watcher event. A second log_note with the same title writes slug-1.md beside the first. Deletion is a move to .trash/ by the CLI, by Obsidian, or by the agent through move_notes; the watcher or a prune then removes the chunks and sweeps Related links to the note

Scoping model.value: None. One vault per install, shared by every agent and every project the user works on; the only predicate on the read path is the optional frontmatter type, a taxonomy chosen by the writer

Agent integration.value: A stdio or streamable-HTTP MCP server with six tools (search_vault, vault_status, get_connections, move_notes, log_note, suggest_folder); instruction files for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Copilot that make the vault the first memory to search and the authoritative one to write; a typer CLI and launchd or systemd services

Background processing.value: A watchdog observer, run as a login service, that ingests and auto-links every saved note and optionally moves new notes into the folder whose description they best match, rewrites folder descriptions, and spins inbox clusters out into new folders; it does no catch-up on start, so changes made while it is down wait for a manual sync or prune

Trust/provenance model.value: None. A note is believed from the moment it is written; there is no status, no confidence, no provenance beyond the filename, the folder and a frontmatter date, and a note written by an agent is indistinguishable from one written by the user

Notable strengths.value: The store is plain Markdown a person can read, fix and delete in Obsidian, and every fix reaches retrieval on save; deletion is recoverable and sweeps dangling links; the long-lived server reconnects when another process changes the index; the watcher distinguishes an atomic save from a delete

Main risks.value: The 0.35 score floor admits any chunk with cosine above -0.3, so search almost never returns nothing; a second note on the same title stacks instead of correcting; move_notes lets the agent trash notes with no confirmation; the HTTP transport has no authentication and DNS-rebinding protection is off by default; a vault under a dot-directory indexes nothing; search and ingest are untested against a real index

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: A `MemoryRecord`: content, tags, a string-to-string metadata map, one of four tiers (`L0Raw`, `L1Atom`, `L2Scenario`, `L3Project`), a creation time, an optional confidence, a relation list, three access counters, a lifecycle state, and six routing keys — `scope`, `agent_id`, `session_id`, `task_id`, `user_id` and `project`. Its `id` is a SHA-256 over the content, the tier, the node id, and every routing key that is set, so identity is the value together with where it belongs

Storage backend.value: One of four backends behind a `MemoryBackend` trait: Markdown files under a memory directory, sqlite-vec, Qdrant, or TencentDB; a pgvector store sits beside them. Above the store, `headgate` keeps a bounded committed-context state that serialises to a four-file bundle — manifest, schema, snapshot and a `qualify.jsonl` decision log — plus a session anchor in `log.md` and subagent lifecycle receipts in `receipts.jsonl`

Retrieval strategy.value: A hybrid `find`: keyword hits and vector hits merged by the trait's default implementation, with every populated routing key applied as an equality filter first — as a predicate in the files backend, as a `must_eq` in the vector backend's own filter — and a state predicate that admits only `Active` unless `include_archived` is set. A decay function over last access and access count computes a retrieval strength used for ranking and eviction, `mmr` diversifies, and `neighbors` and `by_entity` walk relations as separate calls rather than as an arm of `find`

Write strategy.value: `memory.store` over MCP or `artesian memory store` on the CLI. The write is synchronous and local: no LLM call, no embedding service unless the configured backend needs one. Identity is computed first, and an existing record with the same id short-circuits the write and returns what is already there. A per-session lane lock serialises concurrent writes to one collection. The files backend appends a line to `log.md` naming the stored id and node

Update/delete model.value: Three exits. `artesian memory retract` sets `Retracted`, stamps `retracted_at`, adds a `superseded_by` relation and stores a separate retraction record naming the retracted node — the original stays readable through `get_node` and through a query with `include_archived`. `artesian memory evict` archives by TTL, LRU, minimum strength or a keep cap, hard-deletes already-archived records when asked, and appends every decision to `~/.artesian/eviction.jsonl`. Neither is exposed over MCP: an agent can write and read, and only a person at a terminal can retract or evict

Scoping model.value: Six keys on the record and the same six on the query. `MemoryScope` is a four-value enum; `agent_id`, `session_id`, `task_id`, `user_id` and `project` are free strings. A populated query key excludes every record that does not match it, and the project filter is a union that admits the shared project beside the named one. The keys also enter the record's identity hash, so the same sentence stored under two projects is two records rather than one

Agent integration.value: An MCP server exposing twenty-eight tools, nine of them memory: `memory.find`, `memory.store`, `memory.answer`, `memory.context`, `memory.anchor.get`, `memory.anchor.set`, `memory.session.checkpoint`, `memory.session.resume` and `agents.list`; the rest are orchestration and team coordination. A CLI with `init`, `memory store|find|retract|evict`, `tokens`, `perf` and `doctor`. Python bindings, a Homebrew tap, a Dockerfile

Background processing.value: No daemon is required for memory. Decay is computed at read time rather than swept; eviction, consolidation, backfill and the `dream` pass are commands a person runs. `headgate` compresses and evicts the committed context inline when the token budget saturates, and the process agent can run an autonomous loop with a declared budget envelope

Trust/provenance model.value: `MemoryState` is the epistemic field and it filters; `confidence` is an optional float and it ranks. The qualify gate carries a `ReasonCode` enum — qualified, below-relevance-threshold, redundant, stale-version, budget-saturated, drift, gate-rejected — on every admit and reject. Subagent spawns are fail-closed behind a receipt when `ARTESIAN_RECEIPTS_FAIL_CLOSED` is set, and consolidation and the LLM judge are opt-in

Notable strengths.value: A scope key that both backends apply inside their own filter rather than after it, with a CI gate that proves the isolation against two present controls; identity that hashes the routing keys alongside the content, so a memory cannot leak across a project by being a duplicate; retraction that withholds without deleting and stays readable for drill-down; an eviction log that records the reason and the retrieval strength behind every archive and delete; destructive operations kept off the agent-facing tool surface

Main risks.value: Eviction — and therefore the whole audit log — constructs a `FilesBackend` unconditionally, so on the sqlite-vec backend the README recommends, nothing decays, nothing is archived and the log stays empty; the eviction log records the computed plan rather than the applied outcome, and the apply step counts its own successes separately; the `qualify.jsonl` and `lifecycle.jsonl` the README calls an append-only audit log are written with `std::fs::write`, which truncates, so they are snapshots of an in-memory vector; the OCF spec files the receipt and bundle code say they mirror exactly are not in this repository; retraction blocks a re-store only because identity is a content hash, so a paraphrase re-enters as `Active`; no validity time anywhere, so a memory that was true last quarter and false now has no way to say so

Memory unit.value: Several: an asset row keyed on its value; an exploration node (goal, intent, fact, finding, hint, digest) with a state and a server-stamped origin; a coverage row per surface and risk area; and a lesson, a kind, cue and action built by string rules from one finding, with a status and evidence rows

Storage backend.value: PostgreSQL: one global assets table, per-task exploration nodes and edges with anchors to assets, a coverage ledger with a history table, three lesson tables; content-addressed files for captured request and response evidence

Retrieval strategy.value: No search engine. Each planner round is rebuilt from windowed newest-first reads of the task's graph with cursors and digests for the rest; lessons are one SQL query filtered by company, category and status, capped at eight rows with no cursor

Write strategy.value: Agent tools write assets, facts, findings and coverage; a person sets a finding's disposition over an authenticated route; lessons are extracted by rule when a disposition changes, a retest completes or the task ends, with no model call

Update/delete model.value: Asset upserts overwrite scalars and union arrays with no history; facts are append-only; cold regions are folded into digests that keep their members; a changed disposition marks a lesson's evidence row withdrawn in the same transaction, retires the lesson at zero live rows, and reopens a goal the finding had proved; a lesson has no edit or delete path

Scoping model.value: A task reads assets inside its scope rows and graph nodes of itself plus at most eight direct source tasks; a lesson is served to tasks of its company and category, and a company-less lesson to every company-less task. Agent integration.value: A Go server with an embedded web UI; planner, worker, retester and platform agents on an external agent SDK; lessons framed in the nonce envelope and appended to the planner and worker system prompts when an environment flag is set

Background processing.value: A compaction pass folds settled graph regions into model-written digests; lesson extraction runs inside a disposition change and a completed retest, and after a terminal task status

Trust/provenance model.value: A finding's disposition is set by a person, gates which lesson is built, is copied onto the node the agents read, and is refused as goal proof when false positive, duplicate or ignored, reopening a goal it had proved; a lesson is `candidate` or `retired` and the selection excludes retired rows; a fact carries a provenance the server computes from recorded activity, and an unverified fact proves nothing

Notable strengths.value: Explicit one-hop task inheritance that is read-only by construction and tested negatively, a nonce-framed envelope for stored text re-entering prompts, digests that hide and never delete, evidence bound to captured traffic, and lessons and goals that lose their support in the transaction that reverses the verdict behind them

Main risks.value: The planner holds a tool that writes the scope rows its own asset and lesson reads follow; lessons of tasks declared by domain alone form one pool shared by every such task; a fact the agent labels as operator input skips the provenance check and can prove a goal; no lesson can be edited or deleted

Memory unit.value: An RDF subject in an `ops:` ontology of about twenty declared classes — `Decision`, `Task`, `Goal`, `Handoff`, `Person`, `Project`, `Entity`, `Reminder` and the rest — carrying `ops:createdAt`, an unvalidated `ops:status`, and typed edges, beside AST-derived entities for the workspace's own code (functions, callers, imports, dependents) mapped by a tree-sitter pass

Retrieval strategy.value: SPARQL against the tier's store, composed per hook moment rather than ranked: session start returns the working set, the active notes and the handoffs, the prompt hook returns matching domain rules and prior decisions, the pre-tool hook returns the rules and shape of the file about to be read, and the post-tool hook returns the call chain for the lines just returned. A `FILTER NOT EXISTS { ?x ops:supersededBy ?y }` is spliced into recall, both rules blocks and the prompt neighbourhood; the session-start memory block and `learn --list` select `status active` instead, which the supersession writer leaves in place

Write strategy.value: Synchronous CLI and hook writes under a file lock, loaded and mutated inside the lock, serialised to a temp file and renamed atomically; the changes line and a doorbell notification to any running app both fire after the rename lands, never before

Update/delete model.value: Correction is a supersession edge and nothing is re-pointed: `new ops:supersedes old` with the inverse and a `superseded` status in one INSERT, A→B→C left as three records and two edges, `resolve_head` walking forward to the live end, and `would_cycle` refusing a loop at write time. The INSERT adds the status without deleting `active`, and the sync of `domains.toml` deletes every triple on a synced rule, the edge included. Removal is a separate verb whose guard and DELETE ask the same wildcard question

Scoping model.value: Two tiers as two files, selected by `find_workspace_base(cwd)`, and per-workspace named graphs inside a tier that writes are routed to and no hook query filters on. One read-path predicate exists: the session-start working set keeps projects whose `ops:path` resolves to the current registered workspace or to none. Notes, rules, decisions, tasks and handoffs are read across every named graph in the tier

Agent integration.value: A single Rust binary wired into all four Claude Code hooks — session start, prompt submit, pre-tool, post-tool — installed by a shell or PowerShell one-liner, plus a CLI of graph verbs, a Svelte dashboard, a doorbell socket for a running Electron app, and a plugin and extension surface. Hook output is trimmed to a byte budget before it is printed. Codex and Antigravity are named as coming

Background processing.value: None on a timer. Session start runs three passes: graph compaction when a tier has grown past a threshold, backup-first and cooldown-gated; an archive of reminders ten days past due; and a deferral pass over cold handoffs, forks, tasks and milestones, gated on `[defer] enabled`, false by default. The supersession audit runs inside `base doctor` rather than at write time

Trust/provenance model.value: Provenance is the changes log and the supersession chain. `ops:status` is a lifecycle label — six declared values, 44 in the author's measured store — that the working set and the memory block filter on; no value separates a candidate from a verified record

Notable strengths.value: The source comments are incident records: a dated quad count proving a declared predicate had never been written, a status-value census that explains why the label is not trusted, a numbered bug where a wildcard guard and a scoped DELETE disagreed, and tests that name the release they were red at and carry a control that must stay green

Main risks.value: The session-start memory block serves a superseded note beside its correction, because it filters on a status the supersession writer adds to rather than replaces. Memory unit.value: A conversation frame — the user query and the agent's final answer concatenated, titled with the session id and a timestamp

Storage backend.value: One Memvid `.mv2` file per tenant and session, named `agent_{tenant}_session_{session}.mv2` under a base directory

Retrieval strategy.value: Delegated to Memvid's own search, exposed as a single agent tool taking a query string

Write strategy.value: One commit per completed turn from the swarm overseer, with failures logged and swallowed

Update/delete model.value: None found — the wrapper appends, and exposes no delete, supersede or retire path

Scoping model.value: The tenant and session are the filename, so separation is a file boundary rather than a predicate

Agent integration.value: A tool named `memvid_agent_memory_search`, registered on the agent builder alongside the other tools

Background processing.value: None in the memory path

Trust/provenance model.value: None in the memory path; the runtime's guardrails and RL audit trail sit elsewhere in the tree

Notable strengths.value: The wrapper is small enough to read in one sitting and does the honest thing at both ends: the search tool and the commit are constructed from the same `(tenant_id, session_id.unwrap_or("anon"))` pair, so what an agent can read is exactly what this runtime wrote for it — there is no asymmetry between the write key and the read key, which is the bug this shape usually has. A commit failure is logged at error level rather than propagated, so a memory write cannot fail a user's turn. And the wider runtime is candid about its own staging: `INTEGRATION_STATUS.md`, `PHASE_A_SUMMARY.md` and `COMPLETION_SUMMARY.md` sit at the top level, which tells a reader which parts are finished before they go looking

Main risks.value: The tool's description tells the model it is searching "your absolute long-term memory for past conversations, facts, or context you have stored", and the store it reaches is one file per session. Past conversations therefore means earlier turns of the current conversation — unless the session id is absent, in which case both the write and the read fall back to the literal `"anon"` and a tenant's whole session-less history pools into a single shared file, which is the only configuration in which the description is accurate. Nothing in the 148-line layer supersedes, retires or de-duplicates: each turn appends the query and the answer concatenated, so a fact restated ten times is ten frames, and there is no delete path at all. Scope is the filename rather than a predicate, which is the physical-partition shape this atlas does not count as enforcement. The tree also carries `.backup` copies of two source files committed beside their originals in `src/`

Memory unit.value: A chunk with an embedding, an importance score, two lifecycle columns, hormonal and somatic scalars, a sensitivity tag and a provenance chain; above it a canonical fact addressed by key; beside it entities and relationships in a knowledge graph

Storage backend.value: One SQLite database with sqlite-vec vectors and FTS5, carrying `chunks`, `canonical_facts`, `canonical_conflicts`, `entities`, `relationships`, `memory_audit_log`, and dream, curiosity and skill tables; a full reindex rebuilds the index tables and copies every other table across

Retrieval strategy.value: Hybrid vector and lexical fused by reciprocal rank, with graph expansion, recency and mood-congruent boosts and a retrieval trace; the search SQL filters on model and source only, so lifecycle reaches it through index membership; canonical facts bypass retrieval and are injected by key

Write strategy.value: Session extraction into chunks written with a pending embedding until a backfill pass, a canonical ledger with a closed op set of ADD, STRENGTHEN, SUPERSEDE and REJECT, and a curiosity loop that closes the previous answer's validity window; the similarity conflict resolver has no caller

Update/delete model.value: Consolidation marks chunks expired and forgotten and merges losers under a parent; a purge sweep hard-deletes forgotten and expired rows and their vector and FTS rows once `updated_at` is older than the retention; the owner can edit a chunk's text or hard-delete it from all three tables at once

Scoping model.value: None in the memory store — one owner per database. A guest turn filters search hits to rows whose stored and recomputed sensitivity are both normal, which is a sensitivity label rather than a scope key

Agent integration.value: A local gateway on one port serving a Control UI with a Memory page for listing, editing, forgetting, retiring facts and export; memory_search, memory_get and memory_pin tools for the agent; channels including WhatsApp, browser automation via Playwright, a P2P skills marketplace and a wallet

Background processing.value: A dream engine with modes, an oscillator, an adaptive interval and a self-evaluator that grades dreaming by whether its results get used; plus consolidation and purge every maintenance tick, embedding backfill, health sweeps, a curiosity loop with web research, and epistemic directives

Trust/provenance model.value: Canonical status active, retired or superseded gating injection; two chunk lifecycle columns read through one predicate on skill, listing and backfill paths; an append-only audit table written per caller; provenance chains; lineage, structural and entity-admission gates on the graph; a sensitivity filter on guest turns

Notable strengths.value: The canonical ledger answers a real failure of similarity-gated stores — short high-importance facts share no embedding mass with a cold first message — by addressing them by key and injecting them unconditionally, with a closed op set and deterministic score-based demotion. The project acted on a published finding within weeks with a shared liveness predicate, a repair migration, a test seeded so the old filter would fail, and a source-scanning test for cross-vocabulary comparisons. Owner forget deletes from the table and both indexes in one transaction and says in its own comment why a soft mark would not do

Main risks.value: The hybrid search SQL reads neither lifecycle column, so a chunk consolidation forgets stays retrievable until the purge deletes its index rows. The relationship validity interval is stamped with the insert time and closed at supersession time by every writer, so the graph records when it believed a fact and not when the fact held; the as-of reads that use it have no caller outside tests. The vocabulary test matches only `col <op> 'literal'`, and `conflict-resolver.ts` compares `lifecycle` with `forgotten` inside a COALESCE it does not see. A full reindex restores a demoted chunk's `lifecycle` without its `lifecycle_state`. An owner-retired fact is reactivated by the next same-value pin, including the agent's

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: Two units. A 256-byte run receipt: step count, exit flag, maze identity and up to six landmark events with cell and direction. And a plan row: situation hash, action ids, provenance hash and a truth state

Storage backend.value: A fixed 4,128-byte binary ring of 16 receipts plus a derived priors text file in the user data folder, and an append-only JSONL file whose rows are chained by SHA-256, writable only under a scratch/rl/ path

Retrieval strategy.value: Exact key only. The ledger is filtered by maze hash and grid cell and counted per direction; the plan store is matched on a SHA-256 of task, observation tokens, weights hash and domain version. No ranking, text search or embedding

Write strategy.value: The harness writes one receipt at the end of each model run from four code-detected triggers. Plan rows are written between runs by a seeding mode of a test binary, from an oracle walk that reached the exit. The model writes neither

Update/delete model.value: No update or delete verb on either store. The ring overwrites its oldest slot on the seventeenth write; plan rows are never changed, and editing one breaks the chain and turns the whole store off

Scoping model.value: Ledger lookups for a decision are filtered by the maze's hash. The 384-token prompt block is not. The plan key includes the model weights hash and a domain version

Agent integration.value: Compiled into the maze drivers. A dead-end direction keeps 1/(1+n) of its search prior; a plan hit moves half the root prior mass to one edge after legality and gate checks. A prompt block exists behind an off-by-default flag

Background processing.value: None. Receipts are written at run teardown and read as a snapshot at the next run's start

Trust/provenance model.value: Plan rows carry Unverified, SimVerified, HumanVerified or Refuted, and a policy flag sets the floor for a hit. Receipts have no state. A memory-informed run appends the ledger snapshot's SHA-256 to its hash chain

Notable strengths.value: Memory can only reweight a search that still checks legality and the gate; reads come from a hashed snapshot so a run replays from bytes; mid-run writes are refused; a broken chain fails closed; misses are kept like successes

Main risks.value: Only the first five non-exit events of a run are kept, so late dead ends are never remembered; sixteen runs on other mazes evict a maze's memory; a later Refuted row cannot retire a verified one; the chain is unkeyed and has no stored head

Memory unit.value: A Markdown document at a file-like path in one workspace, stored as numbered revisions; each revision carries body, author, reason and a list of source strings, and a deletion is a revision with an empty body and a deleted flag

Storage backend.value: One SQLite database: knowledge_docs with UNIQUE (workspace, path, revision), where the current document is the highest revision; a separate workspace_audit table logs workspace and channel changes and is never read

Retrieval strategy.value: No ranking and no prompt injection: a bot lists current documents, fetches one by path, or filters by a case-insensitive substring over paths and bodies; the guide tells it to start from INDEX.md, and channels point at paths, some marked mandatory

Write strategy.value: Synchronous HTTP PUT with the revision the writer read; a stale base revision is a 409 and the bot must re-read and merge; any bot of the workspace, any human and any admin bot may write, with no approval step

Update/delete model.value: Update is a new revision; DELETE appends a deleted revision and leaves every earlier body readable through history and ?revision=N; only deleting the whole workspace removes rows

Scoping model.value: workspace_id on every row and in every query, taken from the bot's token; admin bots and humans name a workspace; anonymous reads are allowed by default and see every workspace

Agent integration.value: A FastAPI board with a REST API and web pages; bin/bot launches Claude Code, Codex, Copilot or OpenCode sessions that read the guide and call the API with a per-bot token

Background processing.value: No pass over the knowledge base ships; a reconciler is described as a routine an admin bot writes on request and a human approves, and its prompt is not in the tree

Trust/provenance model.value: No epistemic state: every current revision is equally authoritative; settled versus open decisions, and contradictions, are rules in the bot guide's prose

Notable strengths.value: Compare-and-set writes that refuse a lost update; full revision history with author, reason and sources; scope derived from the token rather than the request; a deletion that keeps history

Main risks.value: The workspace boundary is cooperative: an anonymous read or a re-registered human handle crosses it; a deleted document can be recreated by anyone who reads its revision number; deleted bodies stay readable; erasure means deleting the whole workspace

Memory unit.value: A markdown note in an Obsidian vault the operator owns; Brigade keeps only a derived index and proposal staging under its own state directory, owner-readable only

Storage backend.value: The operator's vault for the notes themselves, with an allowlisted set of roots Brigade may index, plus per-operation receipts under a Brigade state directory

Retrieval strategy.value: Index and search over the allowlisted roots, returning cited notes; a separate scenario-driven harness grades projections against named invariants

Write strategy.value: Additive proposals only: a proposal is staged, then delivered into one allowlisted inbox through a symlink-free directory handle, as a planned kernel mutation whose receipt is checked for a committed terminal state

Update/delete model.value: None from the agent's side — it cannot overwrite an existing note and has no delete. What a note becomes is the operator's business in their own editor

Scoping model.value: Allowlisted roots and filesystem containment rather than a stored scope key: paths are opened relative to a directory handle without following symlink components, and an inbox that escapes the vault is refused

Agent integration.value: A CLI with a large command surface, receipts for runs and routes, attestation records, and a skills subsystem with its own proposal inbox

Background processing.value: A projection kernel that prepares, commits and restores multi-file operations, plus memory care planning and closeout passes and a memory doctor

Trust/provenance model.value: None. A note carries no status, no confidence and no validity window; what protects the store is that the agent cannot modify it, not that a memory can be marked doubtful

Notable strengths.value: The agent has a propose verb and no accept verb anywhere in the tree, which is the strongest form of a review gate; the containment refuses to run where its primitives are unavailable rather than falling back to a plain open; the same must-not-exist precondition is enforced both by the file handle and as a plan precondition; the kernel states the guarantee it provides and the stronger one it does not; and the retrieval eval returns a named violation sentence with its hash check written in both directions

Main risks.value: Nothing verifies who accepts a proposal — resolution happens in the operator's editor, so the separation is of surfaces rather than identities; receipts are per-operation artifacts with optional HMAC signing rather than an append-only ledger, and one path unlinks an install receipt; and a note has no status, so a proposal accepted in error is indistinguishable afterwards from one accepted deliberately

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: A per-user fact — key, value, category, type, confidence, both validity bounds, both transaction bounds, a status, a lineage link and an override priority — beside messages, sessions, held intentions and emotional capture

Storage backend.value: PostgreSQL with pgvector for facts and embeddings, Redis for session state, and Neo4j optionally for the knowledge graph

Retrieval strategy.value: Full-text and semantic search over active facts, with relevance scoring, collision handling and a context builder that assembles the prompt block

Write strategy.value: Messages are recorded and facts extracted in the background, with contradiction detection and a quality scorer running over what was written

Update/delete model.value: A correction supersedes: the old row keeps its lineage, takes a status and a `superseded_at`, and a corrections row records both values; nothing is deleted

Scoping model.value: `user_id` stored on every fact and required by every read signature, with `intent_id` as an optional narrower scope for a conversation thread

Agent integration.value: A TypeScript SDK to drop into a chatbot, with a Docker compose stack for the three services it needs

Background processing.value: Multi-stage consolidation, fact extraction, sentiment analysis, response-quality scoring and dedup passes

Trust/provenance model.value: A CHECK-constrained status vocabulary, confidence and override priority on a fact, contradiction detection over active values, and a corrections log with reasons

Notable strengths.value: The migration that introduced the second time axis is the document to read, because it states the problem before the solution: the table already had validity bounds, and "[w]hat was missing is the second time axis — WHEN WE CHANGED OUR BELIEF — distinct from when something was true. Without this you can't honestly answer 'what did we believe about X on date Y' — you can only answer 'what was true on date Y.'" It then defines each of the four columns in a line, writes out the composed predicate, and ships `getFactsAsOf(userId, asOfValidTime, asOfTxnTime)` with both instants defaulting to now — so the ordinary read and the historical read are the same code path with different arguments, and the historical one cannot rot separately. The status vocabulary is enforced by a `CHECK` rather than by application code, and the partial index is built on `WHERE fact_status = 'active'`, which makes the active set the read set at the planner level as well as in the predicate

Main risks.value: The corrections log carries `old_value` and `new_value` in the clear, which is what makes the lineage answerable and also means an erasure request has to reach the corrections table as well as the fact — the opposite trade from the one argued a report earlier, and there is no purge path here that reaches both. Nothing is keyed on a rejected value, so a corrected fact can be re-extracted from a later message and written again as active. There is no human surface: this is an SDK, corrections come from extraction and contradiction detection rather than from a person, and the `reason` on a correction row is a fixed string chosen by the code ("Value correction", "Temporary override") rather than an explanation anybody wrote. The committed tests are unit-level — SQL shape, context formatting, consolidation gating — with no store-level case asserting that a superseded or another user's fact fails to come back, which is the assertion this design would most benefit from pinning. And the runtime is three services: Postgres with pgvector, Redis, and Neo4j when the graph is on

It then defines each column in one line apiece and writes the composed query out. `getFactsAsOf(userId, asOfValidTime, asOfTxnTime)` implements exactly that, with the two predicates carrying their own comments — "transaction-time: known to us, not yet superseded as of asOfTxnTime" against "valid-time: was true in the world at asOfValidTime" — and both parameters defaulting to now, so the ordinary call is the point-in-time call with today's instants | the axes are fed from different places: `recorded_at` is stamped by the write and `superseded_at` by `NOW()` at the moment of belief change, while `valid_from`/`valid_until` are carried through extraction as the fact's own claim about the world

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: Two units. A `knowledge_base_document_chunk` — a row carrying `vectorStoreId` and a `FileEntry` pointer, with the text in file storage and the embedding in pgvector, so one chunk exists in three stores at once. And a Spring AI `Message` in a conversation, addressed by a `conversationId` the workflow author types

Storage backend.value: Postgres for rows plus a `kb_`-prefixed pgvector table for embeddings, chunk text in pluggable file storage, and chat memory in whichever of nine backends the workflow wires up — JDBC, Redis, MongoDB, Cassandra, Neo4j, S3, in-memory, a vector store, or the built-in application database

Retrieval strategy.value: Vector similarity only, `topK` 10 by default, through `KnowledgeBaseVectorStoreWrapper`, which AND-s `knowledge_base_id` and any tag filter onto the request. Chat memory is `MessageWindowChatMemory` — the last N messages of one conversation, no search. There is no lexical arm and no fusion

Write strategy.value: Upload a document and a message-broker worker runs read → split → embed asynchronously, flipping the document through UPLOADED, PROCESSING, READY and ERROR. Chat messages are written by the Spring AI advisor chain during the call

Update/delete model.value: Real and thorough at the chunk and document level: deleting a document removes its vectors, its chunk content files, its chunk rows, its source file and its row, in that order, inside one `@Transactional` facade. Editing a chunk re-embeds it asynchronously. A conversation is deleted whole by `deleteConversation`. Nothing is keyed on a value and there is no tombstone

Scoping model.value: `knowledge_base_id` is a stored key AND-ed into every vector search. Around it sit two ThreadLocals — `TenantContext`, selecting a Postgres schema and defaulting to `public`, and `EnvironmentContext`, selecting model credentials and defaulting to `PRODUCTION`. Chat memory has no scope key at all: `findConversationIds()` returns every conversation in the store

Agent integration.value: Memory is a cluster element inside a visual AI-agent node — the author drops in a chat-memory component, a knowledge base, a document retriever and guardrails, and wires them. Also a REST API, a GraphQL API and an embeddable SDK

Background processing.value: A message-broker worker owns the whole ingest path and the re-embed after a chunk edit. No pass re-reads or rewrites the store on a schedule

Trust/provenance model.value: None over memory content. `KnowledgeBaseDocument.status` is a pipeline stage — UPLOADED, PROCESSING, READY, ERROR — recorded on the document, and no read path consults it, so a chunk whose re-embed failed answers queries with its pre-edit embedding while the document reads ERROR in the UI

Notable strengths.value: `SanitizeTextAdvisor.getOrder()` returns `DEFAULT_CHAT_MEMORY_PRECEDENCE_ORDER - 1`, so PII and secret masking runs one step ahead of the chat-memory advisor and what is persisted is the masked text — asserted by a test whose message says so; the runtime refuses to start an agent with two guardrails of the same kind, because two advisors at one order make the ordering undefined

Main risks.value: Both ambient scopes fail open to a real target rather than closed — an unbound thread reads the `public` schema and the `PRODUCTION` environment, and the S3 chat memory will *create* a `<prefix>-public` bucket for it; the conversation id is an address rather than a permission, and the workflow editor offers a dropdown of every conversation in the store labelled with its opening line

Memory unit.value: A thought node — content, a type, a domain, a storage timestamp and an optional `referent_time` event clock, an access count and last-accessed stamp, a source file, tags, a mood state, a `decayed` flag and a `permanent` flag — linked by derivation edges

Retrieval strategy.value: Similarity search over embeddings plus graph traversal along derivation edges, every path excluding decayed nodes on both endpoints, with a gentle recency weight in [0.5, 1.0] computed from the event clock

Write strategy.value: Extractors pull nodes from conversations and files; a sleep protocol consolidates, cross-links and garbage-collects in a work-capped vectorised pipeline

Update/delete model.value: Decay rather than deletion — the row and its content stay, the flag is set, and an audit row records the transition; a frequently-read node is promoted to permanent and exempted from decay for good

Scoping model.value: A domain field on each node and a single per-user database; no scope predicate is applied on the read path

Agent integration.value: A CLI, a daemon, extractors for agent transcripts, a dashboard, and skills and integration directories for wiring an agent to the graph

Background processing.value: The sleep protocol — consolidation, cross-linking, permanence promotion, decay and audit garbage collection — in a batched, Numpy-backed pipeline with configurable work caps

Trust/provenance model.value: No epistemic state. Access count is the signal that matters: it drives promotion to permanent and it gates decay, and a node that was read even once is out of the decay set entirely

Notable strengths.value: A decay gate that requires a node to be old, never read, and orphaned in the *live* subgraph before it can be forgotten, with cascading held to a stricter threshold and a single live parent enough to save a child; an audit helper that snapshots the node on the caller's connection so the record and the state change commit together; and an event clock the operational passes are forbidden by docstring from reading

Main risks.value: Decay is keyed on the row and never consulted on the write path, so re-extracting a decayed sentence produces a fresh node with no trace of the first; the decay audit is itself garbage-collected, so the record of a forgetting has a retention of its own; `permanent` is irreversible by design, so a node promoted by a burst of reads can never be demoted; and there is no scope predicate — the boundary is one database per user, which makes the domain field a label rather than a partition

project_benchmark_results.note: Profile descriptions and Atlas capability evidence are not benchmark results.

Memory unit.value: A memory row with content, one of fourteen `memory_type` values, one of eight statuses, one of three visibility tiers, a `tenant_id`, `fleet_id` and `agent_id`, a content hash, a `ts_valid_start`/`ts_valid_end` window, a nullable `confidence`, an `is_inferred` flag, a JSONB `scope` of structured validity qualifiers, a `supersedes_id`, recall counters, a soft-delete stamp and an optional RDF triple projection of subject entity, predicate and object

Storage backend.value: PostgreSQL with pgvector at 1,024 dimensions (BAAI/bge-m3) and a `tsvector` column for full text, under Alembic migrations past number forty. Four services — `core-api`, `core-storage-api`, `core-worker`, `core-operations` — plus a plugin and TypeScript and Python clients. Docker Compose for development, with an optional local reranker

Retrieval strategy.value: A hybrid SQL search: vector similarity and full-text score combined in an `ingredients` CTE, with tenant, fleet and visibility as hard predicates and status restricted to the three live values. Soft multipliers handle what hard filters would over-prune — a lapsed `ts_valid_end` applies a currency factor rather than excluding the row, and a date range boosts rather than filters. An optional rerank pass and a `valid_at` parameter for historical questions

Write strategy.value: `caura_write` over MCP or the HTTP API takes plain text; an enrichment step classifies the memory type and may downgrade the status to `cancelled` or `conflicted`. Three types — `outcome`, `rule`, `insight` — are server-reserved: agents may not supply them at the write boundary, the enrichment prompt omits them from the offered vocabulary, and `_validate_enrichment` demotes any that slips through to the default type. A live-content-hash unique index keyed on tenant, fleet, agent and hash enforces the dedup contract the write path advertises

Update/delete model.value: A soft `deleted_at` plus five non-live statuses. Contradiction handling is a unified model: `confidence` guards the invariant that weak evidence must not delete strong, `is_inferred` stops a materialised memory silently overriding a stated fact, and the JSONB `scope` means two memories conflict only when their validity qualifiers overlap. A crystallizer deduplicates and archives losers. Rejecting a distilled skill writes its cluster fingerprint to a poison table with a cooloff, which the next distillation run consults

Scoping model.value: Three keys and a tier. `tenant_id` is mandatory, `fleet_id` optional, `agent_id` recorded on every row, and `visibility` is `scope_agent`, `scope_team` or `scope_org`. `_fleet_scope_clause` is the single builder every fleet-scoped read calls, with a strict mode that excludes fleetless rows and an org-visibility disjunct that survives strict mode because it is a tier a writer chose rather than an accident of a missing fleet

Agent integration.value: Sixteen MCP tools including `caura_write`, `caura_recall`, `caura_evolve`, `caura_insights`, `caura_keystones`, `caura_doc`, `caura_manage`, `caura_tune` and `caura_stats`; an HTTP API; a plugin; TypeScript and Python clients on npm and PyPI. The old `memclaw_*` tool names, environment variables and URLs keep working after the rename

Background processing.value: A worker for enrichment and embedding; a crystallizer that deduplicates and consolidates; an evolve service that turns outcomes into rules; an insights service; a Forge cron that clusters memories into candidate skills and files them to the inbox; an async audit flush that batches chained appends

Trust/provenance model.value: Eight statuses of which three are live; a nullable `confidence` in the claim rather than in the retrieval; `is_inferred` distinguishing a materialised memory from a stated one; three server-reserved memory types agents cannot mint; a per-tenant tamper-evident audit chain; a human inbox in front of every distilled skill; and a poison table that remembers a rejected fingerprint for a cooloff window

Notable strengths.value: Every one of the seven mechanisms this atlas grades for is present, wired to a reachable path, and tested; a rejection record keyed on the value and consulted before the next proposal, which almost nothing here has; an audit chain whose serialisation point is a separate one-row-per-tenant table so the log never takes the lock; one shared visibility clause written after a leak moved from one copy of a predicate to the next; a write boundary that refuses to let an agent mint the three types the server derives

Main risks.value: The poison record expires — a rejected fingerprint is skipped for a cooloff of thirty days by default and is proposable again after it, so the tombstone is a moratorium rather than a permanent refusal; the inbox and the poison table both sit behind an `org_settings.skills_factory.enabled` flag and return 403 when it is off; the accuracy numbers in `BENCHMARKS.md` are not reproducible from this tree, which the file says itself; the surface is large enough that a self-hosting team is adopting four services, a worker and a migration chain past forty rather than a library
